title: Minimum Number of Moves to Make Palindrome
statement:
You get a string `s` of lowercase English letters. In a single move you may exchange any two characters that sit next to each other in `s`. Return the smallest number of moves after which `s` reads the same forwards and backwards.

The input is guaranteed to be rearrangeable into a palindrome, so an answer always exists.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
s can be turned into a palindrome (at most one letter occurs an odd number of times)
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every sequence of swaps (a breadth-first search over arrangements) is correct but explodes with the length. Instead, settle the string from the outside in. The leftmost character has to end up paired with an equal letter at the far right. Keeping `chars[left]` where it is and dragging the nearest equal letter from the right costs exactly the distance to `right`, and it never hurts the inner part: every swap made only shifts letters that stay inside. Once the two ends match, they can be ignored and the same reasoning repeats on the shorter middle.

The single letter with an odd count has no partner and belongs in the centre. If it shows up at `left`, push it one step inward (one move) and try again with the new letter at `left`.

## Approach

1. Copy `s` into the array `chars`, set `moves = 0`, `left = 0`, `right = n - 1`.
2. While `left < right`, scan `match` leftward from `right` until `chars[match]` equals `chars[left]`.
3. If `match === left`, the letter is the lone middle one: swap it with its right neighbour, add one move, and repeat the step without moving the pointers.
4. Otherwise move the letter at `match` to position `right` (that is `right - match` adjacent swaps), add that to `moves`, and shrink the window with `left++` and `right--`.
5. Return `moves`.

## Example 1, step by step

`chars = [a, a, b, b]`, `left = 0`, `right = 3`. Scanning from the right, the first `a` is at `match = 1`. Moving it to index 3 costs `3 - 1 = 2` moves and gives `[a, b, b, a]`. Now `left = 1`, `right = 2` and `chars[2]` already equals `chars[1]`, costing `0`. The pointers cross, so the answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): each of the n/2 rounds scans and shifts at most n characters.
- Space: O(n) for the character array.

## Pitfalls

- Match the left letter with the **nearest** equal letter scanning from the right; picking another one wastes swaps.
- Do not advance `left` or `right` after handling the lone middle letter; the new `chars[left]` still needs a partner.
- Moving the letter costs `right - match` moves, not 1; count every adjacent swap.
- Strings are immutable in JavaScript, so work on an array.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `chars` | the string as a mutable array of letters |
| `moves` | adjacent swaps used so far |
| `left`, `right` | the outer positions still to be settled |
| `match` | position of the nearest letter equal to `chars[left]`, scanning from `right` |
| `lone` | the unpaired middle letter while it is swapped inward |
| `moved` | the letter taken out at `match` and reinserted at `right` |
